title: Numbering the commandments
hookLine: Catholics and Lutherans number them one way, Orthodox and Reformed another; the words are the same

cards: Ask a few Christians to recite the second commandment, and you may get two different answers, each said with total confidence. One says: no graven images. Another says: don't take the Lord's name in vain.
Neither has misremembered. They grew up in churches that count differently. Catholics and Lutherans number the commandments one way.
Orthodox and Reformed Christians number them another. Day 394 walked through the ten words themselves; today, why the Bible lets the counting differ.

teach.b: Open Exodus 20 and look for the numbers. There aren't any. The passage runs from "I am the LORD thy God" to the warning about coveting your neighbor's house, wife, servants, ox and donkey, as one unbroken speech.

What the Bible does give is the total. Later in Exodus, the tablets carry "the words of the covenant, the ten commandments." In the Hebrew, that phrase reads, literally, the ten words, which is today's line.
So: ten. But where do the cuts go?

Catholics and Lutherans, following a division tradition credits to Augustine, keep no other gods and no carved images together as the first word, then split coveting in two at the end: your neighbor's wife, then your neighbor's goods.
Orthodox and Reformed Christians, and Anglicans with them, make images a word of its own and keep coveting together as the last.
Jewish tradition counts another way again: its first word is God's own introduction, I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of Egypt. Each pattern underlines something.
Setting images apart puts weight on how God is worshipped. Splitting coveting, some readers say, makes clear that a person is not a possession.
Starting with I am says the law begins with who God is and what God has done, before any rule.
Whichever way a church counts, every word is still read.
The words on the tablets are the same words; only the dividing lines move.

how: Christians learn the Ten Commandments in catechism, Sunday school and confirmation classes, and each tradition teaches its own numbering: Catholic and Lutheran catechisms one way, Orthodox, Reformed and Anglican teaching another.

games.q: you're dividing Exodus 20 into ten. you reach the end: don't covet your neighbor's house, wife, servants, ox or donkey. one word, or two?
o: one word: coveting is one desire.
two words: a person and a possession are different.
either one: the text gives no numbers.
games.why: Exodus gives no numbers. Orthodox and Reformed Christians keep coveting as one word; Catholics and Lutherans make it two. both read every word.

practice: If you have a Bible or a phone nearby, read Exodus 20, the first seventeen verses, slowly, once, without numbering anything; just notice where you'd put the breaks.
If the text isn't to hand, say the ones you remember, in whatever order they come, and notice which come to you first.

wordCard.voice: Numbering the commandments. The same ten words, divided in different places by different churches, with every word kept.
